findings.issue_text: src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:74 — get_committable_offsets() builds list(self.all_offsets.keys()) with no lock while add_offset() (line 56-60) can concurrently insert a brand-new partition key into the same defaultdict under only that partition's lock, risking "dictionary changed size during iteration" (swallowed by the commit loop's broad except, causing a skipped commit cycle)

src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:191 — get_queue_for_group() uses Python's built-in hash() on group_key, whose value is randomized per-process (PYTHONHASHSEED); assignment is stable within a single run but differs across restarts, so a group's queue affinity is not reproducible run-to-run (only a design nit, not a within-run correctness break)

src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:125 — OrderedQueueWorker.shutdown` is a boolean flag while `FixedQueuePool.shutdown` (line 231) is a method that flips that flag and stops the pool, so the same identifier means two different things across closely related classes

src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/result_consumer.py:206 — create_thread_parallel_worker` (batched-parallel mode) and `create_thread_queue_parallel_worker` (thread-queue-parallel mode) both implement "group by `build_payload_grouping_key`, parallelize across groups, preserve intra-group order" via two unrelated mechanisms (batch+ThreadPoolExecutor vs. persistent hash-routed queue workers), duplicating a concept without a shared abstraction, which will make it unclear to future readers which mode to extend

src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/result_consumer.py:136 — num_queues=max_workers or 20` silently repurposes the `max_workers` CLI option (originally documented for thread pool size) as a queue count, with an inline magic default of 20 instead of a named constant

src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:214 — get_stats()` returns `dict[str, Any]` exposing a raw `queue_depths` list of ints rather than a typed structure (dataclass/TypedDict), leaking internal representation to callers like `poll()` and `wait_until_empty()

src/sentry/consumers/__init__.py:121 — Adding "thread-queue-parallel" alongside existing "parallel" (multiprocess) and "batched-parallel" (ThreadPoolExecutor) modes, whose internal handler is literally named `create_thread_parallel_worker`, compounds pre-existing inconsistent mode naming and makes the three parallel strategies harder to tell apart by name alone

src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/result_consumer.py:180 — SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()/terminate() shuts down the factory's shared FixedQueuePool, but create_with_partitions (called by arroyo on every rebalance) reuses that same shared self.queue_pool for the next strategy instance, so after the first rebalance all workers/queues are permanently dead and subsequent submits are silently dropped or raise queue.ShutDown

src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:154 — OrderedQueueWorker.run() has no restart/health-check: if an exception escapes except Exception (e.g. BaseException) the thread dies permanently while items already/still enqueued to that queue are never processed, so their offsets never complete and commits for that partition stall forever with no visible failure beyond a log line

src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:255 — SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() joins commit_thread and queue_pool.shutdown() joins each worker with only a 5s timeout; if a worker is stuck in a long-running result_processor call, join() silently times out, the thread is leaked, and any offsets it was mid-processing never complete/commit before the process exits, risking reprocessing on restart

src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:274 — commit_loop's while loop only rechecks shutdown_event after the 1s wait, so one extra get_committable_offsets/commit_function call executes after shutdown is requested; this is likely intended but is undocumented and not obviously safe if commit_function itself is mid-shutdown-sensitive

tests/sentry/uptime/consumers/test_results_consumer.py:1922 — test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling's assert (`len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets`) only passes because the wait-loop breaks almost instantly (processing is synchronous/mocked) before the commit thread's first 1.0s tick (queue_consumer.py:276 `shutdown_event.wait(1.0)`); since `OrderedQueueWorker.run()`'s `finally` (queue_consumer.py:148-149) unconditionally calls `complete_offset` even after an exception, the failed offset 100 *will* be committed once the periodic commit loop fires, so this test is a timing race that gives a false-negative pass and does not actually prove failures block commits

src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:212 — FixedQueuePool.get_queue_for_group` does `hash(group_key) % self.num_queues` which raises ZeroDivisionError if num_queues==0 (or produces a negative index for weird hash values), and no test in test_queue_consumer.py or result_consumer wiring covers num_queues<=0 or a negative/zero max_workers passed through `max_workers or 20` in result_consumer.py

src/sentry/consumers/__init__.py:121 — No test exercises the new `thread-queue-parallel` click.Choice value wired through uptime_options()/get_stream_processor CLI options (no tests/sentry/consumers directory exists), so a regression removing or mis-wiring the CLI option would not be caught

src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:148 — No test kills/crashes an OrderedQueueWorker thread itself (e.g. an exception raised outside the inner try, such as from `offset_tracker.complete_offset` in the `finally`, or from `work_queue.get()`) to verify recovery/no-recovery — since there is no restart logic for dead worker threads, a worker that dies leaves its queue permanently stuck with no test coverage of this reliability risk

tests/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/test_queue_consumer.py:202 — test_stats_reporting's assertion `len(stats["queue_depths"]) == 3` only checks the FixedQueuePool constructor's num_queues value, not any real per-queue distribution/depth behavior, so it would pass trivially even if depths were computed incorrectly

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:74 — get_committable_offsets() builds list(self.all_offsets.keys()) with no lock while add_offset() (line 56-60) can concurrently insert a brand-new partition key into the same defaultdict under only that partition's lock, risking "dictionary changed size during iteration" (swallowed by the commit loop's broad except, causing a skipped commit cycle)

adjudication.rationale: In OffsetTracker.get_committable_offsets(), it does `for partition in list(self.all_offsets.keys()):` without any global lock protecting `self.all_offsets`. Meanwhile, add_offset() can concurrently create a new key in `self.all_offsets` (it’s a defaultdict) under only a per-partition lock (which doesn’t exist yet for a brand-new partition until created). That allows the underlying dict to be resized while `list(self.all_offsets.keys())` is iterating, which can raise `RuntimeError: dictionary changed size during iteration`. The commit thread’s broad `except Exception` in `_commit_loop` would swallow it and skip a commit cycle, matching the finding.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:191 — get_queue_for_group() uses Python's built-in hash() on group_key, whose value is randomized per-process (PYTHONHASHSEED); assignment is stable within a single run but differs across restarts, so a group's queue affinity is not reproducible run-to-run (only a design nit, not a within-run correctness break)

adjudication.rationale: In `FixedQueuePool.get_queue_for_group` the diff shows `return hash(group_key) % self.num_queues`, which relies on Python’s built-in `hash()` for a `str`. Python string hashing is salted per process by default (PYTHONHASHSEED), so the queue index for a given `group_key` will be stable within a single process run but can change across restarts. That doesn’t break within-run ordering guarantees (items for a group still always map to the same queue during that run), but it does mean queue affinity/load distribution isn’t reproducible run-to-run, which is a valid design/ops concern rather than a direct correctness bug.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:125 — OrderedQueueWorker.shutdown` is a boolean flag while `FixedQueuePool.shutdown` (line 231) is a method that flips that flag and stops the pool, so the same identifier means two different things across closely related classes

adjudication.rationale: In the diff, `OrderedQueueWorker` defines an instance attribute `self.shutdown = False` (a boolean flag) and checks it in `run()` (`while not self.shutdown:`). Separately, `FixedQueuePool` defines a `shutdown(self) -> None` method that sets `worker.shutdown = True` for each worker. This is not a functional defect by itself (the code is consistent and works), but it is a concrete, diff-grounded maintainability issue: the same identifier `shutdown` refers to a method on the pool and a boolean flag on the worker in closely related classes, which is easy to misread and can lead to mistakes when extending/refactoring (e.g., thinking `worker.shutdown()` exists).

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/result_consumer.py:206 — create_thread_parallel_worker` (batched-parallel mode) and `create_thread_queue_parallel_worker` (thread-queue-parallel mode) both implement "group by `build_payload_grouping_key`, parallelize across groups, preserve intra-group order" via two unrelated mechanisms (batch+ThreadPoolExecutor vs. persistent hash-routed queue workers), duplicating a concept without a shared abstraction, which will make it unclear to future readers which mode to extend

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds a new processing mode (`thread-queue-parallel`) in `ResultsStrategyFactory` that, like the existing `batched-parallel` path, groups by `build_payload_grouping_key` and parallelizes across groups while preserving per-group order, but does so via a separate mechanism (`FixedQueuePool` + `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` in `create_thread_queue_parallel_worker`). The existing `batched-parallel` implementation achieves similar semantics through batch partitioning + `ThreadPoolExecutor` (`create_thread_parallel_worker` calling `partition_message_batch`). This is a diff-grounded architecture/maintainability concern (two unrelated implementations of the same conceptual mode), not a concrete correctness defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/result_consumer.py:136 — num_queues=max_workers or 20` silently repurposes the `max_workers` CLI option (originally documented for thread pool size) as a queue count, with an inline magic default of 20 instead of a named constant

adjudication.rationale: In `ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__`, the new `thread-queue-parallel` branch constructs `FixedQueuePool(..., num_queues=max_workers or 20, ...)`, which does indeed reuse the `max_workers` setting as a queue-count/parallelism control and hardcodes `20` inline despite `FixedQueuePool` already having a `num_queues: int = 20` default. This is a concrete maintainability/clarity issue (parameter semantics + magic default), not a correctness defect, and it’s test-backed as intentional behavior (e.g., `assert factory.queue_pool.num_queues == 5`). Also, it is not entirely “silent” since the CLI help text for `--max-workers` was broadened to “parallelism” in the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:214 — get_stats()` returns `dict[str, Any]` exposing a raw `queue_depths` list of ints rather than a typed structure (dataclass/TypedDict), leaking internal representation to callers like `poll()` and `wait_until_empty()

adjudication.rationale: `FixedQueuePool.get_stats` does return `dict[str, Any]` with a raw `queue_depths: list[int]`, but this is a typing/API-design nit rather than a verifiable defect or meaningful review issue. In the diff, the only callers are internal (`poll`, `wait_until_empty`) and tests; nothing indicates this “leaks” a problematic internal representation or causes incorrect behavior.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/consumers/__init__.py:121 — Adding "thread-queue-parallel" alongside existing "parallel" (multiprocess) and "batched-parallel" (ThreadPoolExecutor) modes, whose internal handler is literally named `create_thread_parallel_worker`, compounds pre-existing inconsistent mode naming and makes the three parallel strategies harder to tell apart by name alone

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds a new CLI mode string "thread-queue-parallel" in `src/sentry/consumers/__init__.py` and wires it up in `ResultsStrategyFactory` (`mode: Literal[...]` plus `create_thread_queue_parallel_worker`). The existing mode naming is already somewhat inconsistent: `mode == "batched-parallel"` routes to a method named `create_thread_parallel_worker` (see `create_with_partitions`), while `mode == "parallel"` routes to `create_multiprocess_worker`. Adding another parallel-sounding mode string does make it harder to distinguish the strategies by name alone, but this is a clarity/maintainability concern rather than a correctness defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/result_consumer.py:180 — SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()/terminate() shuts down the factory's shared FixedQueuePool, but create_with_partitions (called by arroyo on every rebalance) reuses that same shared self.queue_pool for the next strategy instance, so after the first rebalance all workers/queues are permanently dead and subsequent submits are silently dropped or raise queue.ShutDown

adjudication.rationale: In `ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__`, `mode == "thread-queue-parallel"` creates a single shared `self.queue_pool = FixedQueuePool(...)`. `create_thread_queue_parallel_worker` then reuses that same `self.queue_pool` for each new `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy`. However, `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()` and `terminate()` both call `self.queue_pool.shutdown()`, which shuts down all underlying `queue.Queue` instances via `q.shutdown(...)` and stops/join worker threads. After that, a subsequent rebalance that calls `create_with_partitions` again will reuse the already-shutdown `self.queue_pool` (factory does not recreate it), so future `submit()` calls will enqueue into shutdown queues (likely raising `queue.ShutDown`) and workers are no longer running. This matches the finding’s described failure mode.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:154 — OrderedQueueWorker.run() has no restart/health-check: if an exception escapes except Exception (e.g. BaseException) the thread dies permanently while items already/still enqueued to that queue are never processed, so their offsets never complete and commits for that partition stall forever with no visible failure beyond a log line

adjudication.rationale: In `OrderedQueueWorker.run`, the worker loop only catches `queue.ShutDown` and `Exception`. Any `BaseException` (e.g. `SystemExit`, `KeyboardInterrupt`, potentially other non-`Exception` throwables) raised during `result_processor(...)` or surrounding code would terminate the thread, and there is no health-check/restart logic in `FixedQueuePool` to recreate it. If that happens mid-processing, the `finally` block won’t run, so `offset_tracker.complete_offset(...)` isn’t called for that work item; `OffsetTracker.outstanding` would retain the offset and `get_committable_offsets()` would stop advancing commits for that partition. This is a robustness/liveness concern visible in the diff, though it depends on rare exception types; also the finding’s “beyond a log line” part isn’t guaranteed because `BaseException` wouldn’t be logged here.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:255 — SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() joins commit_thread and queue_pool.shutdown() joins each worker with only a 5s timeout; if a worker is stuck in a long-running result_processor call, join() silently times out, the thread is leaked, and any offsets it was mid-processing never complete/commit before the process exits, risking reprocessing on restart

adjudication.rationale: In the newly added queue_consumer implementation, `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()` sets `shutdown_event`, then `join()`s `commit_thread` with a 5s timeout, and calls `FixedQueuePool.shutdown()`, which sets `worker.shutdown = True`, calls `q.shutdown(immediate=False)`, and then `worker.join(timeout=5.0)` without checking whether the thread actually exited. `OrderedQueueWorker.run()` cannot be interrupted while inside `self.result_processor(...)`; `worker.shutdown` is only checked at the top of the loop, and `queue.shutdown()` only affects `work_queue.get()`. If `result_processor` blocks/long-runs, `join(timeout=5.0)` can time out and `close()` returns with a still-running daemon worker. Because `complete_offset(...)` is only called in the worker's `finally`, a stuck worker never marks the offset complete, and since the commit loop is stopped by `shutdown_event`, that offset cannot become committable/committed before process exit, leading to uncommitted in-flight work and reprocessing on restart.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:274 — commit_loop's while loop only rechecks shutdown_event after the 1s wait, so one extra get_committable_offsets/commit_function call executes after shutdown is requested; this is likely intended but is undocumented and not obviously safe if commit_function itself is mid-shutdown-sensitive

adjudication.rationale: In `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy._commit_loop`, the loop condition is checked only at the top (`while not self.shutdown_event.is_set():`). Inside the loop it calls `self.shutdown_event.wait(1.0)` but does not re-check the event afterward, so if shutdown is set during/just before the wait returns, that iteration still runs `get_committable_offsets()` and may call `commit_function(committable)` once after shutdown has been requested. This is a real, diff-grounded behavioral edge case; it’s not clearly a correctness defect (could be intentional to commit final offsets), but it is not documented and could be problematic if `commit_function` is not shutdown-safe.

adjudication_records.issue_text: tests/sentry/uptime/consumers/test_results_consumer.py:1922 — test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling's assert (`len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets`) only passes because the wait-loop breaks almost instantly (processing is synchronous/mocked) before the commit thread's first 1.0s tick (queue_consumer.py:276 `shutdown_event.wait(1.0)`); since `OrderedQueueWorker.run()`'s `finally` (queue_consumer.py:148-149) unconditionally calls `complete_offset` even after an exception, the failed offset 100 *will* be committed once the periodic commit loop fires, so this test is a timing race that gives a false-negative pass and does not actually prove failures block commits

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces a real correctness bug: `OrderedQueueWorker.run()` unconditionally calls `self.offset_tracker.complete_offset(...)` in its `finally` block even when `result_processor(...)` raises (queue_consumer.py around the `except Exception`/`finally`). Since `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy._commit_loop()` periodically commits any offsets that are no longer outstanding (after `shutdown_event.wait(1.0)`), a failed message will still be considered “completed” and become committable, causing the consumer to commit past a failed offset (data loss / skipped retry) despite the strategy docstring claiming “Only commits offsets after successful processing.” The finding is also correct that `test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling` is a timing race: it breaks once the queues drain (often <1s with mocks) and asserts no commits before the commit thread’s first 1s tick, so it can pass even though a commit would occur shortly after.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:212 — FixedQueuePool.get_queue_for_group` does `hash(group_key) % self.num_queues` which raises ZeroDivisionError if num_queues==0 (or produces a negative index for weird hash values), and no test in test_queue_consumer.py or result_consumer wiring covers num_queues<=0 or a negative/zero max_workers passed through `max_workers or 20` in result_consumer.py

adjudication.rationale: In the new `FixedQueuePool` (src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py), `get_queue_for_group` returns `hash(group_key) % self.num_queues` with no validation that `num_queues > 0`. If `num_queues == 0`, this will raise `ZeroDivisionError`. Additionally, `__init__` builds queues/workers via `for i in range(num_queues)`: if `num_queues <= 0` (e.g., a negative `max_workers` passed through `num_queues=max_workers or 20` in result_consumer.py, where negative values are truthy), the pool will have zero queues and `submit` will later index into an empty list (`self.queues[queue_index]`). The finding’s “negative index from weird hash values” part is inaccurate (Python `%` with positive divisor yields a non-negative remainder), but the unhandled `num_queues <= 0` case is a real defect exposed by this diff and is not covered by the added tests.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/consumers/__init__.py:121 — No test exercises the new `thread-queue-parallel` click.Choice value wired through uptime_options()/get_stream_processor CLI options (no tests/sentry/consumers directory exists), so a regression removing or mis-wiring the CLI option would not be caught

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds a new CLI option value `thread-queue-parallel` to `click.Choice([...])` in `src/sentry/consumers/__init__.py` via `uptime_options()`, but the tests added/modified in this PR focus on the new queue processing strategy and uptime consumer behavior (`tests/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/test_queue_consumer.py` and additions in `tests/sentry/uptime/consumers/test_results_consumer.py`). The diff does not include any test that exercises the CLI parsing/wiring of the new click choice through the consumer CLI entrypoints, so a future regression in the CLI option wiring would not be caught by tests shown here.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:148 — No test kills/crashes an OrderedQueueWorker thread itself (e.g. an exception raised outside the inner try, such as from `offset_tracker.complete_offset` in the `finally`, or from `work_queue.get()`) to verify recovery/no-recovery — since there is no restart logic for dead worker threads, a worker that dies leaves its queue permanently stuck with no test coverage of this reliability risk

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces long-lived daemon worker threads (OrderedQueueWorker) in a FixedQueuePool with no supervision/restart mechanism (workers are started once in FixedQueuePool.__init__ and only joined on shutdown). If a worker thread terminates unexpectedly, its dedicated queue will no longer be drained. While OrderedQueueWorker catches exceptions from result_processor, exceptions in `work_queue.get()` beyond `queue.ShutDown`, or in the `finally` block (`offset_tracker.complete_offset(...)` / `metrics.gauge(...)`) would escape and could kill the thread. The added tests cover ordering, committing, and basic error handling, but none simulates or asserts behavior when a worker thread dies, so this reliability risk is not exercised.

adjudication_records.issue_text: tests/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/test_queue_consumer.py:202 — test_stats_reporting's assertion `len(stats["queue_depths"]) == 3` only checks the FixedQueuePool constructor's num_queues value, not any real per-queue distribution/depth behavior, so it would pass trivially even if depths were computed incorrectly

adjudication.rationale: In `test_stats_reporting`, the assertion `len(stats["queue_depths"]) == 3` (after `stats = self.pool.get_stats()`) only verifies that `get_stats()` returns a list with one entry per queue, which will naturally match `FixedQueuePool(num_queues=3)` as long as it iterates `self.queues`. It does not validate that the per-queue depths are correct or reflect any meaningful distribution/behavior (e.g., that the queue receiving work shows increased depth). So the finding is a valid, diff-grounded critique of test strength rather than a product bug.
